set.approach: From the Evans Creek mouth near Slocan, take the Beatrice Lake trail, which climbs steeply at first and then eases. Continue past Emerald Lake, with another short steep rise beyond its western shore, and reach Cahill Lake inside Valhalla Provincial Park. The route is on the large south-facing slab of a gneiss dome on the lake's north shore, below the sub-peaks of Hela Peak, and the wall is a short walk from the camping area at the lake's western end.
set.descent_text: The route finishes near the top of the dome. Descend by walking down talus to an unnamed creek, then return to the Cahill Lake campground. The talus is slow in the dark, so carry a headlamp.

review.notes: Single article on the first ascent: Beatrice Lake trail via Cahill Lake, dome on north shore, talus descent to a creek. No counts or times used.

set.approach: Both approaches start on the Anderson River forest road, where a damaged bridge stops vehicles. The quickest way in leaves the southern branch of the road and follows the stream draining westward off the peak's southern flank, roughly 4 km beyond the bridge. Climb very steep dirt beside a waterfall on its north side to old-growth forest (a fixed hand line helps), then continue on easy walking in the old forest up to the base of the southeast col. The climb begins at the Ibex and Steinbok col, a little left of the crest of the ridge.
set.descent_text: The usual way down is to rappel the route. The anchors are typically slung trees, so carry your own webbing and rap rings, since old slings may be chewed or weak.

review.notes: Area page gives the creek approach to the southeast col; route page gives the start at the col and the rappel-the-route descent.

set.approach: Both approaches start on the Anderson River forest road, where a damaged bridge stops vehicles. The quickest way in leaves the southern branch of the road and follows the stream draining westward off the peak's southern flank, roughly 4 km beyond the bridge. Climb very steep dirt beside a waterfall on its north side to old-growth forest (a fixed hand line helps), then continue on easy walking in the old forest up to the base of the southeast col. The ridge starts down and to the right of the Ibex and Steinbok col, on the crest of a long buttress.

review.notes: Approach from the area page; start position from the route page. Route page says it ends on the upper North Ridge but not how parties descend, so no descent written.

set.approach: Approach through the Tantalus Range to the Lycia and Serratus col, and cross it to the Ionia Glacier. Cross the ice to the foot of the Ionia buttress, at its far right edge where the snow meets rock. The route climbs the northeast side of the peak from there.

review.notes: Route page location text; no clear descent (a bolted rappel line is mentioned but not located), so no descent written.

set.approach: This ridge is reached most easily by following the ridge line south from Green Mountain, which curves round to become the east ridge of Mount Land. It can also be reached from the middle Ault Lake. The ridge steepens into scrambling to a first notch.

review.notes: Area and route pages agree on the Green Mountain ridge approach and the Ault Lake alternative.

set.approach: The standard base is the Hind hut, among the highest huts in the range, which is booked through the Assiniboine lodge; tenting nearby may also be allowed. The hut is reached by the steep ledge system known as Gmoser's Highway, which has a cliff-band traverse where a roped fall could be dangerous, so have the rack ready. From the hut, cross the moraines to the foot of the north ridge and follow the easy lower crest, staying right of the snow, along the easy lower part of the ridge, then work left across snow to get around the lowest cliff band.
set.descent_text: Descend by careful downclimbing with some rappels from the many fixed anchors, although not every anchor is used. Pulling rappel ropes can knock down rock, so move cautiously, tell other parties what you are doing, and wait in safe spots on a busy day. Trapdoor cornices on the summit ridge have claimed lives, so stay back from the edge.

review.notes: Single route page, standard route description. Row grade (5.4) differs slightly from the 5.5 seen elsewhere; same line.

set.approach: Drive to the Chehalis Lake road and park near a large water bar. Walk the road, crossing a creek on an old bridge or by rock-hopping, then turn left at a cairn or flagging onto the trail to lower Statlu Lake. Walk around the lake past the signed turnoff to upper Statlu Lake and the Viennese-Clarke traverse, staying left. Beyond the lake the trail fades into bushwhacking: head west toward the talus on the far side of the creek, pick up a faint trail, and continue north toward Bardean and Ratney. Climb the slash at the toe of the feature, bypass a slot canyon with snow, and climb a short pitch up a face to a bushy ledge. Cross snow and wet slabs to the bivy basin below the wall. The route begins up a corner system toward the right end of the base.
set.descent_text: From the top, walk the ridgeline toward Ratney and descend into the col, then scramble through blocks just left of the first big snow patch to the summit of Ratney. From there skirt the snow heading northeast toward the rib on the north end of the basin that holds lower Statlu Lake. Rappel anchors start near a possible cairn, and the old slings need reinforcing, so carry spare webbing. Several rappels reach the flatter, snowy part of the ridge, then more lead to a ledge with two snow patches on the second southern-facing offshoot, and a last rappel from a tree puts you on the slabs. Snow and wet slabs lead back to camp.

review.notes: One detailed route page. Rappel counts left out (only one source).

set.approach: The Bush River road begins near Donald, and the Rice Brook road branches off at the 98 km sign. It ends at a closure where the old logging road is no longer maintained, so hike the overgrown road, crossing the creek at an old bridge site (an easier crossing may be found a little upstream). Continue along the overgrown road to a moraine crossing and then a last stretch of logging track. From the end of the logging, a long cross-country climb gains the crest of the northeast ridge, well up the mountain. The ridge crosses the Northeast and Central peaks before the true summit.

review.notes: Route page text only. Gain and distances omitted (one source). No descent in sources, so none written.

set.approach: The route is on the cliff that is visible above the Rice Creek forest road, so it is reached from the road in a short walk. Park beside the cliff and hike up to the base of the central weakness in the wall.
set.descent_text: Follow the obvious ledge that leads climber's left until you reach a tree with rappel tat. Rappel from the tree, then use fixed nuts for the next anchor, which takes you across the gully. A third rappel from fixed nuts reaches a grassy slope, from which you hike down to a tree with tat and make the last rappel to the ground. Carry two 60 m ropes.

review.notes: Route page. NOTE: this is a cliff above the Rice Creek road, not on Mount Bryce itself (misfiled under the peak area). Rappel count not stated.

set.approach: From the Lions Bay parking area at the north end of Sunset Drive, hike the steep road up through the switchbacks, passing the signed spur for Brunswick Mountain. Take the unsigned spur road on the left, a few hundred metres farther along, which serves the climbing routes on Mount Harvey and is below the signed Mount Harvey hiking trail. It narrows to a trail that reaches a talus field; rack up here, because the descent comes back down this talus. Cross the lower talus, then climb up and left to the obvious North Face Ramp. Follow the ramp to the level base of the big gully (the gut) that separates Harvey's Pup from Mount Harvey. The route starts on top of a chockstone in the ramp and heads toward a small bush on the right side of a roof.
set.descent_text: The route ends on the summit of Harvey's Pup, a detached pinnacle. From the top, continue east over the summit and find a rappel anchor on a tree; it may be possible to downclimb to the left instead. Scramble down a treed ledge to a second tree anchor and rappel into the notch between the Pup and Mount Harvey. Before reaching the bottom of the notch, walk along a ledge on the Mount Harvey side to the top of the real descent gully. Descend the gully by loose downclimbing, with rappels to avoid steeper sections and some 4th-class steps, until you reach the approach trail where it meets the talus. The rock is loose and many anchors are suspect, so back them up and bring spare rings and carabiners.

review.notes: Route and area pages. Rappel lengths and counts left out (one source).

set.approach: Leave the car on the highway's south shoulder, east of the Hermit lot and short of the avalanche snowshed. A downed log beside the parking spot crosses Connaught Creek. Follow the creek downstream, then angle toward the mountain through a bushwhack with devil's club to the Herdman Couloir. Climb the couloir, which is moderate with an axe and crampons when snow-filled and an unpleasant scramble when dry; it holds snow into early summer. Check the avalanche forecast. Leave the couloir and angle left toward the ridge, passing an obvious ledge for bivouacs just left of the couloir, then scramble steep, treed ground up to a conspicuous notch where the roped route begins.
set.descent_text: From the summit block, which may need one rappel from fixed tat if it is not dry, go down the southwest ridge, which is mostly fourth class, using rappels from slung anchors where needed. At the bottom of the ridge, either cut right into the steep Banana Couloir (one rappel from a large slung block gets you in) or keep going down into the gentler Herdman Couloir. From the foot of the upper couloirs, return to the bivy ledge terrain, descend the lower Herdman, and retrace the bushwhack and log crossing to the road. Both couloirs see rockfall and slides when the sun is on them, so descending in the heat of the day is risky. Check the avalanche forecast.

review.notes: One detailed trip report. Counts of rappels, times, and distances omitted; no testimony used.
